name: Deathstep - detuned FM growl (Operator)
description: Reference checklist for the deathstep mid bass: an inharmonic two-operator FM growl, a formant stage, heavy staged saturation, pitch-drop accents over a chromatic phrase, and a separate sub. Not executable: the engine cannot create Operator patches on Live 12.2.5.

manual.instruction: Build a two-operator FM pair: Osc A sine at 0 dB, Osc B sine modulating it at Coarse 3-8, and a short decay on B's envelope so the modulation is strongest at the attack. Do not use a whole-number ratio if you want it ugly.
manual.verify: One note has a metallic, biting attack that decays into a body.
manual.why: FM drum and bass guidance uses exactly this pair; detuning B off a whole-number ratio is what makes the harmonics inharmonic.

manual.instruction: Route the pair through a formant stage: a narrow band-pass in Auto Filter, or Corpus tuned to a low vowel, swept slowly across the note. Deathstep reads as a voice in pain, not a clean sub.
manual.verify: The growl has a vowel-like centre that moves, and it changes character with the sweep.
manual.why: Genre descriptions name formant filtering as a deathstep bass ingredient alongside FM and wavetable synthesis.

manual.instruction: Split the low end before distortion: filter the growl at about 100-120 Hz so the distortion has no sub to chew, and keep a separate clean sine sub under it.
manual.verify: The distorted growl keeps its weight, and the low end does not turn to mush when drive is added.
manual.why: Distorting a full-range bass makes the fundamental intermodulate; every heavy-bass guide splits the sub first.

manual.instruction: Stack drive in two stages with different characters, for example Saturator (Analog Clip) into Redux or Erosion, then EQ Eight to remove the harsh 2-5 kHz peak the stack created.
manual.verify: The growl is loud and torn but does not make the ears ring on its own.
manual.why: Stacking distortion types is the standard way to get complexity without one stage doing all the work.

manual.instruction: Write a chromatic, dissonant phrase: minor-second moves, a pitch drop at the end of a bar, and a rest before the next hit. Deathstep leans on tension rather than melody.
manual.verify: The phrase sounds threatening without any reverb or effects carrying it.
manual.why: Deathstep is described as prioritising dissonance and chromatic motion over anthemics.

manual.instruction: Print the growl to audio and resample variations: reverse a tail, pitch a copy down an octave for a drop hit, and keep the live patch for the main phrase.
manual.verify: The drop has several distinct growl events without several live synth instances.
manual.why: Deathstep production is described as heavy audio manipulation and resampling of textures.

notes: Sources: Melodigging's deathstep genre notes (https://www.melodigging.com/genre/deathstep); Recording Arts Canada's TenGraphs interview (https://recordingarts.com/record/introduction-of-deathstep); Garnish Music Production's FM drum/build notes (https://edu.garnishmusicproduction.com/ableton-advanced-fm-making-fm-drum-sounds). The formant and split-chain steps are standard bass-music practice applied to the genre description, not a single transcript. Reference-only.
